extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of Kant; philosophers interested in teleology, theology, and epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting Kant’s standards for proofs of God, the classification of cognisable objects (opinion/fact/faith), limits of theoretical reason, and the role of practical (moral) reason in teleology. Focus is on how proofs should be constructed and what kinds of conviction they can legitimately produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof should convince, not merely persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first requisite for every proof ... It should not persuade, but convince, or at least should tend to conviction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof's ground or conclusion must be an objectively valid, logical ground of cognition rather than a merely subjective (aesthetical) determining ground of assent. Illusory proofs (which exploit subjective propensities to be persuaded) may be useful popularly but are not adequate philosophically; they 'ensnare' the Understanding rather than convince it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate persuasion from conviction; do not conflate physical and moral teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: “the division of the proof into the two dissimilar parts involved in the argument--belonging to physical and moral Teleology respectively--cannot and must not be prevented.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or evaluating a teleological proof, explicitly distinguish what belongs to physical teleology (explanations from nature) and what belongs to moral teleology (practical/moral grounds). Blending them hides where the real force of the argument lies and produces wholesome but logically illusory persuasion; philosophers must expose this confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: State whether the proof aims at the object-in-itself or the object-for-us
rubrics_metrics.description: “A proof which is intended to convince ... either deciding what the object is in itself, or what it is for us (proof κατ’ ἀλήθειαν or κατ’ ἄνθρωπον).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs differ in ambition: proofs for determinant (theoretical) judgement attempt to establish what an object is in itself and require adequate theoretical principles; proofs for reflective judgement aim to establish what an object is for us (in light of our cognitive/practical needs) and may rest on practical principles that yield moral conviction rather than theoretical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logically strict syllogistic proofs are inapplicable to supersensible objects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Since no intuition possible for us corresponds to the concept of a Being that is to be sought beyond nature ... there is absolutely no cognition of it to be had.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deductive, universally valid syllogistic proofs require relevant intuitions or empirical correspondence; because supersensible concepts (e.g., God as a being beyond nature) lack any possible corresponding intuition, such logical proofs cannot produce theoretical cognition or belief about them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy-based proofs cannot transfer dissimilar specific determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: “we can indeed think one of two dissimilar things ... according to the analogy of the other; but we cannot, from that wherein they are dissimilar, conclude from the one to the other by analogy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical reasoning can suggest how to conceive a supersensible cause (e.g., by analogy with human understanding), but it cannot legitimately ascribe specific determinations from the analogous (known) case to the disanalogous (supersensible) case. Example: we may analogize divine causality to an Understanding, but cannot infer divine properties in the specific sense we know in humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable opinion requires a completable series of grounds and thus fails for supersensible claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “probability is part of a certainty possible in a certain series of grounds ... the insufficient ground of which must be susceptible of completion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probability presupposes that existing insufficient grounds can be completed into a whole that yields certainty. Empirical grounds that attempt to reach beyond possible experience (to the supersensible) cannot be completed in this way, so 'probability' has no legitimate place in arguments for supersensible objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must rest on a certain possibility; they are unsuitable for supersensible beings
rubrics_metrics.description: “If an hypothesis is to serve for the explanation of the possibility of a given phenomenon, at least its possibility must be completely certain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesis can explain only if the possibility of what it posits is itself certain. Since we lack any criterion that guarantees the possibility of transcendent (supersensible) beings determined by our concepts, hypotheses invoking such beings are groundless for theoretical cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify cognisable things: opinion, fact, and faith
rubrics_metrics.description: “Cognisable things are of three kinds: things of opinion (opinabile); things of fact (scibile); and things of faith (mere credibile).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite classification to evaluate claims: (a) things of opinion are empirically conceivable in principle but inaccessible to us; (b) things of fact have objective reality provable through experience or appropriate intuition (e.g., mathematics); (c) things of faith are required by practical reason (for moral purposes) but are transcendent for theoretical cognition (e.g., God, immortality, the highest good).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thing of opinion: must be at least empirically possible in principle
rubrics_metrics.description: “things of opinion are always Objects of an empirical cognition at least possible in itself ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim counts as an opinion only if, in principle, empirical investigation could settle it (even if practically unreachable). Purely speculative chimeras (e.g., arbitrary disembodied spirits posited without empirical criteria) are not genuine 'opinions' in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thing of fact: objective reality must be provable (theoretical or experiential)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Objects for concepts, whose objective reality can be proved ... are things of fact.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts are those whose objective reality can be demonstrated either by theoretical a priori presentation (e.g., geometry) or by experience/testimony. Kant notes freedom as a special case that can be shown as a fact in practical terms (manifested in actions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thing of faith: moral postulate, not theoretical cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: “Objects ... which in reference to the use of pure practical Reason ... must be thought a priori ... are mere things of faith.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the moral law requires presupposing certain conditions (e.g., the highest good, God, immortality) these are to be accepted as things of faith: they are postulated for the practical use of reason and justified 'adequately for its design' but they do not amount to theoretical knowledge or empirical fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral argument yields practical (moral) conviction, not theoretical proof of God
rubrics_metrics.description: “The actuality of a highest morally-legislating Author is therefore sufficiently established merely for the practical use of our Reason, without determining anything theoretically as regards its being.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant's moral teleology gives us moral grounds to assume a final purpose and thus to postulate God as moral Author of the world for practical ends. This establishes practical reality and duty-oriented conviction, but does not provide theoretical (determinant) knowledge or metaphysical proof of God's being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith as a moral attitude (habitus) justified by obligation to a design
rubrics_metrics.description: “Faith (as habitus, not as act) is the moral attitude of Reason as to belief in that which is unattainable by theoretical cognition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith is a settled moral stance of Reason to assume as true what must be presupposed for the fulfilment of duty (the attainment of a morally commanded final purpose). It is a free belief grounded in practical reason 'adequately for its design,' not empirical testimony or speculative proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosopher’s duty: expose sophistry and put principled bounds on speculative claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “Bounds must then be put to such claims according to a certain principle ... it is the duty of the philosopher ... to expose the above illusion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theological or metaphysical arguments overreach (e.g., by claiming speculative insight into supersensible nature), the philosopher should demand principles that limit such claims and reveal where arguments rely on rhetorical persuasion rather than objective conviction; do not accept failure of past attempts as the only restraint.
